title: The daily prayer for open doors
word: The daily prayer for open doors
hook: for decades the Ardas asked for free access to the gurdwaras left behind

segments.voice: Yesterday, a Punjabi-speaking state: a smaller Punjab, won by peaceful morchas, and your line, the language kept. Today we go back to 1947 one more time, to something Sikhs carried out of it into every single day. Day three hundred four.

Think of a place you can't get back to. A childhood house someone else lives in now. A grandparent's town across an ocean. You can picture the front door exactly, but you can't walk through it. For Sikhs after 1947, that place was Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born, and dozens of other gurdwaras now across a border. And the community did something remarkable with that longing. They didn't just remember it once a year. They put it into the prayer they say every day. Today: the daily prayer for open doors.
screen: `A DOOR YOU CAN'T WALK THROUGH.` → `NANKANA SAHIB, ACROSS THE BORDER.` → `A LONGING PUT INTO A PRAYER.`

segments.voice: You've met the Ardas already: the standing prayer that closes nearly every Sikh gathering. It's said standing, hands joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib. It remembers the ten Gurus, then the Sikhs who gave their lives, then it asks. The Ardas isn't a fixed text from one day in history. Its core is old, and the community has added to it as the story went on. After Partition, a request was added. In plain English, it asks the Guru to grant the Khalsa free sight of, and the care and service of, Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras and holy places from which the Panth has been separated. The Punjabi phrase at its heart is khulle darshan didar: open sight, open visits. So for more than seventy years, in homes and gurdwaras around the world, millions of people have asked, every day, for a door to open. Notice what that does. A loss that could have turned bitter became a daily hope, said out loud, together. The door was not fully shut. Groups of pilgrims, called jathas, were allowed to cross for the big gurpurabs, under agreements between India and Pakistan. But for most Sikhs, a visit to Guru Nanak's birthplace was something you hoped for all your life. Many never went. And still the line was said. The request is in the Ardas today, because Sikhs still ask for open, free access to all the places they were separated from. It's a small lesson in how a community holds a longing: not by forgetting it, and not by letting it harden, but by praying it, gently, every day.
screen: `THE ARDAS: REMEMBER, THEN ASK.` · `A REQUEST ADDED AFTER 1947.` · `KHULLE DARSHAN DIDAR: OPEN SIGHT.` · `A LOSS TURNED INTO DAILY HOPE.` · then, large: `OPEN DOORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold something you've hoped for a long time. Settle, and breathe. Let one long hope come to mind. A reconciliation. A healing. A place you want to see. A door you want opened, for you or for someone else. Don't push it or plan it. Just let it be there. If you pray, you can offer it in your own words, the way the Sikh community has offered its hope for decades. If you don't, simply name it quietly to yourself, and notice how long you've carried it. The bell holds the time.
The daily prayer for open doors. Since Partition, the Ardas has asked for open access to Nankana Sahib and the gurdwaras left behind: khulle darshan didar.
screen: `THE DAILY PRAYER FOR OPEN DOORS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: open doors. Today, open one door for someone else: an invitation, an introduction, a seat at your table. Day three hundred four.

options: stop mentioning the places, so it hurts less.
